clue.text: Study the actual words in their proper setting

parts.note: to con is an old verb for studying or learning by heart
the text of a work is its exact wording

explanation.surface: Advice to a reader: examine the exact wording where it belongs before judging it.
explanation.definitionFit: The surrounding passage that gives words their meaning is the setting in which they properly sit.

clue.text: "Charmed magic —s, opening on the foam Of perilous seas" (Keats)

definitions.text: "Charmed magic —s, opening on the foam Of perilous seas" (Keats)

parts.words: "Charmed magic —s, opening on the foam Of perilous seas" (Keats)
parts.note: the blank is filled from Keats's Ode to a Nightingale, a word for hinged windows

explanation.surface: A line from Keats with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Keats's 'Ode to a Nightingale'; the gap takes a plural, and the answer is its singular.
explanation.definitionFit: A window that opens on side hinges is the kind Keats pictured looking out over the sea.

clue.text: Despite all, nobody gets a smaller quantity

parts.note: none means not one person, nobody
the less is a phrase for a lesser amount

explanation.surface: Even so, no one ends up with less.
explanation.definitionFit: However or even so: carrying on in spite of everything.

clue.text: "Women and wine should life" (Gay)

parts.note: the gap is filled from John Gay's The Beggar's Opera: 'Women and wine should life ...'

explanation.surface: A line from John Gay with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is a song from Gay's 'The Beggar's Opera' (1728).
explanation.definitionFit: To occupy or make use of: wine and women should fill a life.

clue.text: Recorder's tie-up

explanation.surface: The thing that binds a record-keeper's work.
explanation.walkthrough: A recorder (of sound) uses magnetic tape; tape is also a strip for tying things up, as in red tape.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnetic ribbon stores what a recording machine captures; a narrow strip ties up a bundle.

clue.text: Stuck up, these mail users

explanation.surface: A snooty jibe at people who send letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Bills pasted on walls are stuck up; people who send letters by mail post them.

clue.text: Queries tip ?. Anyhow it goes with the job

indicators.note: anyhow means in any old way, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Asking for a tip, as it comes with the work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anyhow' rearranges the letters of QUERIES and TIP together.
explanation.definitionFit: A perk or fringe benefit is an extra that comes along with employment.

clue.text: A stand is made while yet there's time

parts.note: still means yet, as in 'still to come'
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Someone takes a stand while there is still time.
explanation.definitionFit: A stillage is a frame or rack for supporting casks or goods off the floor.

clue.text: Shelter put up for fish

indicators.note: in a down clue put up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: the lee is the side sheltered from the wind

explanation.surface: Building a shelter for a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A long snake-like freshwater and sea creature with fins.

clue.text: Girl with a couple of black eyes

definitions.text: Girl with a couple of black eyes

parts.words: Girl with a couple of black eyes
parts.note: Black-Eyed ... is the heroine of John Gay's ballad and a flower name, so the girl is named for her black eyes

explanation.surface: A girl who has been in a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests bruises; the reference is to 'Black-Eyed Susan', the ballad heroine and the flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Black-eyed Susan is the stock name for the girl in the old sailor's ballad.

clue.text: One Frenchman coming in to eat at dawn

indicators.note: one piece entering another means the French word goes inside the eating word

parts.note: to sup is to eat an evening meal
un is French for one, the word a Frenchman uses for it

explanation.surface: A lone Frenchman arrives early in the morning for breakfast.
explanation.definitionFit: The moment the sun rises over the horizon is daybreak.

clue.text: Very small quantities of soft goods

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for soft
articles are items of merchandise, goods

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper selling only tiny amounts of soft wares.
explanation.definitionFit: Minute bits of matter, specks and grains, are the tiniest portions of anything.

clue.text: Acting crazy, the D.O.M.

indicators.note: crazy says the letters go wild and come out in another order

parts.note: taken as written
D.O.M. stands for Deo Optimo Maximo, or a dirty old man; its letters are D, O and M

explanation.surface: An old man behaving madly on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: THE plus DOM is rearranged by 'crazy'. 'Acting' looks like part of the surface's behaviour but is the definition: the Method is a famous school of acting.
explanation.definitionFit: The Method is Stanislavski's system of acting, where performers draw on real emotion.

clue.text: Gather, love, at Daniel's lodging for battle

parts.note: to cull is to gather or pick out
love is zero in tennis, the letter O
Daniel was thrown into the lions' den in the Bible

explanation.surface: A summons to a sweetheart to meet at Daniel's home before a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: CULLODEN was the 1746 battle in Scotland where the Jacobite rising was crushed.
explanation.definitionFit: Culloden Moor saw the last pitched fight on British soil in 1746.

clue.text: A spirit dies, with differences

annotationWithheld.why: 'A spirit dies, with differences' is an anagram of A SPIRIT DIES with no anagram indicator; 'with differences' would have to be both the definition and the anagram signal

clue.text: Swan and 26 make music, it's punishing !

parts.note: a pen is a female swan
the answer to clue 26, the first part of the name of Ali Baba
to sing is to make music with the voice

explanation.surface: A swan and a friend sing together, and it is painful to hear.
explanation.walkthrough: '26' refers to 26-down, which gives ALI.
explanation.definitionFit: Imposing a penalty on someone is disciplining them.

clue.text: State of one born with very little money

parts.note: née, meaning born, marks the birth name of a person, so it stands for one born
d was the abbreviation for an old British penny, a tiny sum

explanation.surface: A description of someone born into poverty.
explanation.walkthrough: D stood for the old penny in British pre-decimal money.
explanation.definitionFit: Poverty or want is the condition of lacking what one requires.

clue.text: Communiqués get into confusion at times

parts.note: a mess is a state of confusion
ages are long periods, times

explanation.surface: Official statements sometimes become muddled.
explanation.definitionFit: Official bulletins are communications sent from one party to another.

clue.text: Run aground, like a disked celebrity ?

explanation.surface: A famous guest on a radio show finds themselves shipwrecked.
explanation.walkthrough: On BBC radio's 'Desert Island Discs' a celebrity is imagined marooned on an island with a few records.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship run onto the shore is beached; a castaway on a desert island is marooned.

clue.text: Something classic, cased outside, is gently handled

indicators.note: outside means the word 'cased' is placed around the other piece, wrapping it

parts.note: res is Latin, the classical language, for a thing

explanation.surface: A valuable antique, boxed up, is treated with care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classic' means Latin here, the classical language, so 'something' is translated rather than taken as written; 'outside' signals the wrapping.
explanation.definitionFit: Stroked or fondled tenderly, touched with affection.

clue.text: Essential passages?

parts.note: essences drawn out of plants and short excerpts from books are both things taken out

explanation.surface: A question about which parts of a book really matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essential' points to essences such as vanilla, which are drawn out of a source, and 'passages' to excerpts quoted from a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Both concentrates like vanilla essence and quoted excerpts are things drawn out of a larger whole.

clue.text: See 26

parts.note: a cross-reference: this light holds the second half of the name clued at 26-down

explanation.walkthrough: The clue at 26-down covers both lights; this one takes the latter part of the Arabian Nights name.
explanation.definitionFit: The woodcutter hero of the forty thieves tale is named across both lights.

clue.text: A boy in charge of this pile

definitions.note: an adjective describing the pile, the old name for a nuclear reactor

parts.note: Tom is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A boy put in charge of a heap of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pile' looks like a heap but is the old word for a nuclear reactor, the atomic pile.
explanation.definitionFit: Early nuclear reactors were called piles, so this word describes the reactor's kind.

clue.text: Saturday comes round and with it a craze for the Island

indicators.note: turning round means the abbreviation for the weekend day is read backwards

parts.note: a mania is a craze or obsession

explanation.surface: Weekend arrives and everyone suddenly wants to go to the island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comes round' signals a turnaround of the weekday abbreviation; 'and with it' is only a joining phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasmania is the large island state south of mainland Australia.

clue.text: One of which featured inter alia Cowper's sofa

definitions.text: One of which featured inter alia Cowper's sofa

parts.words: One of which featured inter alia Cowper's sofa
parts.note: William Cowper's long poem has a first book titled The Sofa, so the poem is one of these jobs

explanation.surface: A remark about a poet's furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: Cowper's 1785 poem 'The Task' opens with Book I, 'The Sofa', set as a task by Lady Austen.
explanation.definitionFit: Assignments or jobs to be done; Cowper's poem bears the singular as its title.

clue.text: None was worth Landor's

parts.note: Walter Savage Landor wrote 'I strove with none, for none was worth my' and the rhyme word completes the line

explanation.surface: A line from a poet looking back on a life without quarrels.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes Landor's quatrain 'Dying Speech of an Old Philosopher'; the missing final word of the line is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Conflict or contention is what Landor said nobody merited from him.

clue.text: Put nothing on a horse that's mouldy

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece put on another sits above it, so nothing comes first

parts.note: O is the round figure for nothing
gee, or gee-gee, is a child's word for a horse

explanation.surface: Advice not to bet on a horse that is rotten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mouldy' is used in the sense of 'of a moulding': an ogee is an S-shaped moulding.
explanation.definitionFit: An S-curved architectural profile is a type of moulding.

clue.text: Wrapping up the new issue

parts.note: issue means offspring, so the new issue is a newborn baby being bound in cloth

explanation.surface: Finishing work on the latest edition of a magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' reads as a magazine number but means offspring: a new baby being wrapped in bands of cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Tightly binding a newborn in strips of cloth is the old practice of bundling an infant.

clue.text: He had two-score decidedly jarred

parts.note: the hero of the Arabian Nights tale had forty thieves, who hid in oil jars

explanation.surface: Someone had forty men very upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jarred' looks like 'upset' but means put in jars: the forty thieves hid in oil jars and were killed by Morgiana. With 20-across this gives the whole name.
explanation.definitionFit: The woodcutter of the Arabian Nights tale outwitted forty thieves concealed in jars.

clue.text: "Three little from school " (Gilbert)

parts.note: the gap is filled from the song in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado: 'Three little ... from school are we'

explanation.surface: A line from a comic opera with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The song is sung by Yum-Yum, Peep-Bo and Pitti-Sing, three schoolgirls, in The Mikado.
explanation.definitionFit: Young unmarried girls are the trio of schoolgirls singing in the operetta.

clue.text: Hidings give rise to a row

indicators.note: give rise to says the letters produce something new by being rearranged

explanation.surface: Beatings lead to a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of 'Hidings' are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A noisy brawl or rumpus is a lively disturbance.

clue.text: Cut out by the taxman ?

explanation.surface: Something removed by the tax inspector.
explanation.walkthrough: Excise is also a tax on goods, so something 'excised' could be taxed by the excise officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgically removed parts are cut away; excise duty is a tax collected on goods.
